    See the equations behind the diagramsOptional · Nothing moves by guesswork
    GOODS MARKET

    C = c₀ + 0.5Y − r
    I = 35 − 4r
    Y = C + I + G

    These give IS as r = (c₀ + 35 + G)/5 − 0.1Y.

    ASSET MARKET

    M/P = l₀ + 0.8Y − 10r

    More money lowers the rate needed to clear this market. A higher price level reverses that effect.

    FULL EMPLOYMENT

    Y = Y*
    P = M / (l₀ + 0.8Y* − 10r*)

    FE sets long-run output. IS gives r*. Money-market equilibrium then gives P.

    Initial values are c₀ = 15, G = 20, M = 100, l₀ = 60, Y* = 100 and P = 1. Interest rates are expressed in percentage points. Expected inflation is held fixed at zero. These are teaching values, not an estimate of an actual economy.

    SAME COURSE, DIFFERENT ASSUMPTIONS

    Why is SRAS sometimes horizontal and sometimes upward sloping?

    FIXED PRICES

    Firms meet demand at a fixed price.

    SRAS is horizontal. A demand expansion initially raises output. Prices adjust later, bringing output back to full employment.

    MISPERCEPTIONS

    Producers misread an unexpected price change.

    SRAS slopes upward. When P exceeds Pᵉ, producers may mistake a general price rise for a rise in their own relative price and produce more.

    Y = Y* + b(P − Pᵉ), b > 0

    In the misperceptions model, fully anticipated money growth changes expected prices immediately. Unexpected money growth can temporarily raise output. The policy lab above uses the fixed-price setup.
